title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
Directed graphical models

Definition. A directed acyclic graphical model (DAG, or Bayes net) represents each random variable as a node and each assumed direct dependence as a directed edge. A DAG with no cycles implies the factorization p(x_1,\dots,x_N) = \prod_{i=1}^N p\big(x_i \mid \text{parents}(x_i)\big), where \text{parents}(x_i) is the set of nodes with an edge pointing into x_i.

This is the same chain-rule factorization as Why factor the joint, restricted so that each x_i’s conditioning set is only its parents rather than every variable before it in some ordering. A conditional probability table (CPT) stores p(x_i \mid \text{parents}(x_i)): for binary variables, a node with K_i parents needs 2^{K_i} free parameters (one probability per parent configuration, since the two outcomes sum to 1). The total across the graph is roughly N \cdot 2^{\max_i K_i}, which is far smaller than 2^N - 1 whenever the graph is sparse. Restricting every node to a small number of parents is what buys the savings; a fully-connected DAG recovers the general chain rule and its full 2^N-1 parameter cost, with no savings at all.






TipQuestion: Does an arrow in a DAG mean implication, causation, or dependence?





An arrow A\to B means different things in different places, and none of them is by itself a statement about independence. The lecture’s examples (low pressure, rain, traffic, a ballgame, a project deadline, busy forums, a full lab) separate three meanings.
1. Logical implication between events. If A and B are events, A\Rightarrow B means A\subseteq B: whenever A happens, B happens. If rain always caused heavy traffic, the event “rain” would be contained in the event “traffic”, and P(\text{traffic}\mid\text{rain}) = \frac{P(\text{rain}\cap\text{traffic})}{P(\text{rain})} = \frac{P(\text{rain})}{P(\text{rain})} = 1. Independence would need P(\text{traffic}\mid\text{rain}) = P(\text{traffic}), which then forces P(\text{traffic})=1 (or P(\text{rain})=0). So implication is close to the opposite of independence: A tells us everything about B.
2. A causal edge. Reading rain \to traffic causally says traffic is generated from rain plus other inputs: changing the weather would change the traffic. That is a claim about intervening, setting rain by force, which is not the same as observing rain. This chapter’s DAGs only use the factorization, so this causal reading is extra.
3. Dependence is not causation. The lecture’s common-cause example has a project deadline (the shared cause) \to busy forums and deadline \to full lab. Observing busy forums makes a full lab more likely, so the two are dependent. Yet forcing the forums to be busy would do nothing to the lab, because only the deadline affects it. Averaging over the deadline Y with its own distribution, rather than the one implied by the forums, gives the effect of setting the forums X=x on the lab Z: \sum_y P(Z\mid X=x,Y=y)\,P(Y=y) = \sum_y P(Z\mid Y=y)\,P(Y=y) = P(Z). The first equality uses X\perp Z\mid Y from Conditional independence: three canonical structures. The observational P(Z\mid X=x) instead weights each y by P(Y=y\mid X=x), which is why it differs. A shared cause that creates this gap is called a confounder. When the observed variable also has a real effect of its own, confounding can even reverse the apparent direction of that effect, which is Simpson’s paradox.
What an edge does and does not say about the data.

An edge alone constrains nothing. Any joint over two variables factors both ways, p(\text{rain})\,p(\text{traffic}\mid\text{rain}) = p(\text{traffic})\,p(\text{rain}\mid\text{traffic}), so rain \to traffic and traffic \to rain fit the same data equally well.
Missing edges are what constrain. In the chain low pressure \to rain \to traffic, the absent edge from low pressure to traffic is what asserts low pressure \perp traffic \mid rain. Every independence a DAG encodes comes from a missing edge (Conditional independence: three canonical structures).
Causation usually, but not always, produces dependence. If an effect works through two routes that exactly cancel, the variables can be independent despite a causal link. Assuming this never happens is called faithfulness, and only under it does independence rule out a causal effect.
Dependence needs an explanation. If two variables are dependent, then one causes the other or they share a common cause, as busy forums and a full lab share the deadline. Within a data set there is one more source: conditioning on a common effect, as in explaining away, where rain and a ballgame become dependent once we observe the traffic.






  
    
      
    
  
  A DAG and its factorization
  
  x1
  
  x2
  
  x3
  
  x4
  
  x5
  
  x6
  
  
  
  
  
  


Figure 2. A DAG on six nodes. Reading parents off the picture gives the factorization p(x_1,\dots,x_6) = p(x_1)\,p(x_2\mid x_1)\,p(x_3\mid x_1)\,p(x_4\mid x_2)\,p(x_5\mid x_3)\,p(x_6\mid x_2,x_5): each factor’s conditioning set is exactly its incoming arrows, not every earlier node.






Note



Practice question. For the DAG in Figure 2, treat every node as binary. How many parameters does each node’s CPT need, and what is the total across the whole graph? How does that total compare to the 2^6-1 a fully-connected DAG on six nodes would need?
Solution. Read the parent count straight off the arrows into each node: x_1 has no parents (K=0, so 2^0=1 parameter); x_2 and x_3 each have one parent, x_1 (K=1, 2^1=2 parameters each); x_4 has one parent, x_2 (2 parameters); x_5 has one parent, x_3 (2 parameters); x_6 has two parents, x_2 and x_5 (K=2, 2^2=4 parameters). Summing these, 1+2+2+2+2+4=13 parameters for the whole graph, against 2^6-1=63 for the fully-connected case. Compared with the chain rule in the order x_1,\dots,x_6 (costs 1,2,4,8,16,32), every node from x_3 on has fewer parents (costs 1,2,2,2,2,4). The largest single saving is x_6’s CPT, 32 down to 4: it depends on x_2 and x_5 but not on x_1, x_3, or x_4, which is exactly the kind of assumption Why factor the joint said was the only way to cut the parameter count.

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
Conditional independence: three canonical structures

Definition. For disjoint sets of variables A, B, C, we write x_A \perp x_B \mid x_C (“x_A and x_B are conditionally independent given x_C”) if any of the following equivalent conditions hold: p(x_A, x_B \mid x_C) = p(x_A\mid x_C)\,p(x_B\mid x_C), \quad p(x_A\mid x_B, x_C) = p(x_A\mid x_C), \quad p(x_B\mid x_A, x_C) = p(x_B\mid x_C).

A DAG’s edges encode a specific pattern of these independencies. Three three-node structures cover the cases, each checked directly from the factorization it implies.
Causal chain (X \to Y \to Z). The joint factors as p(x)p(y\mid x)p(z\mid y), so p(z\mid x,y) = \frac{p(x)p(y\mid x)p(z\mid y)}{p(x)p(y\mid x)} = p(z\mid y). Once Y is known, X tells us nothing more about Z: X \perp Z \mid Y.
Common cause (X \leftarrow Y \rightarrow Z). The joint factors as p(y)p(x\mid y)p(z\mid y), so p(x,z\mid y) = \frac{p(y)p(x\mid y)p(z\mid y)}{p(y)} = p(x\mid y)\,p(z\mid y). Again X \perp Z \mid Y: two effects of a shared cause become independent once that cause is observed.
Explaining away (X \to Y \leftarrow Z). The joint factors as p(x)p(z)p(y\mid x,z), and now p(z\mid x,y) = \frac{p(x)p(z)p(y\mid x,z)}{p(x)p(y\mid x)} = \frac{p(z)p(y\mid x,z)}{p(y\mid x)} \neq p(z\mid y) in general. X and Z are marginally independent (with Y unobserved), but conditioning on their common effect Y can make them dependent: learning that it rained (X) makes a ballgame (Z) a less likely explanation for heavy traffic (Y), even though rain and ballgames have nothing to do with each other on their own.






Note



Practice question. Three variables from the lecture’s own examples exercise each structure in turn. For each, say which structure it is and whether the two outer variables are independent, both before and after conditioning on the middle one.

Low pressure (X) \to rain (Y) \to traffic (Z).
A project deadline (Y) makes the forums busy (X) and, separately, fills up the lab (Z): X \leftarrow Y \to Z.
Rain (X) and a ballgame (Z) both feed into traffic (Y): X \to Y \leftarrow Z.

Solution.

Causal chain. Marginally, X and Z are dependent (low pressure raises the chance of rain, which raises the chance of traffic). Conditioned on Y (we already know whether it is raining), X tells us nothing more about Z: X \perp Z \mid Y, exactly the causal-chain result above.
Common cause. Marginally, X and Z are dependent: busy forums are a signal that the deadline is near, which makes a full lab more likely too, so the two are correlated through the shared cause even though neither directly affects the other. Conditioned on Y (we already know whether the deadline is near), that shared explanation is used up, and X \perp Z \mid Y.
Explaining away. Marginally, X and Z are independent: whether it rains has nothing to do with whether there is a ballgame. But conditioned on Y (we observe heavy traffic), they become dependent: learning it rained makes the ballgame a less likely explanation for the traffic, and vice versa. This is the one structure where conditioning on the middle node creates a dependency rather than removing one, which is why it is the case worth double-checking whenever a homework or the Bayes Ball algorithm below asks about a head-to-head node.

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
The Bayes Ball algorithm
Checking x_A \perp x_B \mid x_C by hand from the joint, as in Conditional independence: three canonical structures, does not scale: for more than three variables, writing out the full factorization and cancelling terms gets unwieldy fast. D-separation is a purely graph-theoretic condition, built only from paths and arrows, that guarantees conditional independence in every distribution the DAG represents. Unlike the joint-distribution algebra of Conditional independence: three canonical structures, it can be checked by eye on the picture, which is what makes it useful.
D-separation is built from the same three junction types as Conditional independence: three canonical structures, now named for their shape on a path rather than their causal story: a chain node (\to Y \to), a fork node (\leftarrow Y \to, what Conditional independence: three canonical structures called common cause), and a collider node (\to Y \leftarrow, what Conditional independence: three canonical structures called explaining away). Fix a conditioning set C.

Definition. A path between two nodes is blocked by C if it contains at least one node Y where either:

Y is a chain or fork node on that path, and Y \in C (the path is cut at an observed non-collider), or
Y is a collider node on that path, and neither Y nor any descendant of Y is in C (the path is cut at an unobserved collider).

A path that is not blocked is active. Two disjoint sets of nodes A and B are d-separated by C if every path between a node in A and a node in B is blocked by C.

D-separation is a statement about the graph alone, no probabilities involved, which is exactly why it is worth having:

Result. If A and B are d-separated by C, then x_A \perp x_B \mid x_C in every distribution that factorizes according to the DAG. If they are not d-separated, the independence fails in almost every such distribution (it can hold only by an exact cancellation of the numbers in the tables).

This is the fact that licenses reading independence off a picture. The Bayes Ball algorithm is a mechanical way to check d-separation without enumerating every path by hand:






Note



Bayes Ball procedure. To test whether A and B are d-separated by C: shade every node in C (observed). Place a ball at each node in A and let it bounce along edges, obeying the rules below at every node it reaches. If any ball can reach a node in B, some path is active and the graph does not guarantee x_A \perp x_B \mid x_C. If no ball can reach B, every path is blocked and x_A \perp x_B \mid x_C.


The bouncing rules are exactly the blocking condition above, restated as what a ball is and is not allowed to cross:

Chain (\to Y \to): the ball passes through Y if Y is unshaded, and is blocked if Y is shaded.
Fork (\leftarrow Y \to): the ball passes through Y if Y is unshaded, and is blocked if Y is shaded.
Collider (\to Y \leftarrow): the ball is blocked at Y if Y is unshaded, and passes through if Y or any of its descendants is shaded.

That last rule is the one that reverses the usual pattern, and it is exactly the explaining-away asymmetry from Conditional independence: three canonical structures: observing a collider, or anything downstream of it, opens a dependency between its causes that was not there before.
Worked example (from the tutorial). The tutorial’s practice graph has a and f both pointing into e, e pointing into c, and f pointing into b:


  
    
      
    
  
  
    (a) c shaded
    
    
    
    
    
    a
    
    f
    
    e
    
    c
    
    b
  
  
    (b) f shaded
    
    
    
    
    
    a
    
    f
    
    e
    
    c
    
    b
  


Figure 3. The tutorial’s practice graph (a\to e, f\to e, e\to c, f\to b), shaded (grey) nodes are the conditioning set. Panel (a) conditions on c; panel (b) conditions on f.
The only path from a to b is a \to e \leftarrow f \to b, with two junctions to check: e is a collider on this path (both a\to e and f\to e point into it), and f is a fork node on this path (both edges, f\to e and f\to b, point out of f), which blocks under the same rule as a chain: shaded blocks, unshaded passes.
In panel (a), C=\{c\}. At the collider e: is e or a descendant of e in C? Yes, e’s child c is shaded, so the collider is open. At the fork f: is f shaded? No, so the fork is also open. Both junctions on the only path are open, so the path is active: a \not\perp b \mid c. This is worth sitting with, since it runs against plain intuition: shading c, which is not on the direct route between a and f at all, is exactly what creates the dependency, because c is a descendant of the collider e. This is the explaining-away asymmetry from Conditional independence: three canonical structures, one hop removed.
In panel (b), C=\{f\}. At the collider e: neither e nor its descendant c is shaded, so the collider stays blocked, which is already enough to block the whole path regardless of what happens at f. (The fork at f is separately blocked too, since f itself is shaded, but the collider alone already settles it.) So a \perp b \mid f.
Larger example. In the six-node DAG of Figure 2, is x_1 \perp x_6 \mid \{x_2,x_3\}? There are two paths from x_1 to x_6: x_1\to x_2\to x_6 and x_1\to x_3\to x_5\to x_6. On the first path, x_2 is a chain node, and it is shaded, so that path is blocked. On the second, x_3 is a chain node and is also shaded, blocking that path too. Every path is blocked, so yes, x_1 \perp x_6 \mid \{x_2,x_3\}.
Is x_2 \perp x_3 \mid \{x_1,x_6\}? Path 1 is x_2 \leftarrow x_1 \to x_3: x_1 is a fork on this path and is shaded, so this path is blocked. Path 2 is x_2 \to x_6 \leftarrow x_5 \leftarrow x_3: x_6 is a collider on this path (both x_2\to x_6 and x_5\to x_6 point into it), and x_6 is shaded, so the collider is open; continuing along the path, x_5 is a chain node (between x_3\to x_5 and x_5\to x_6) and is unshaded, so it is open too. Both junctions on path 2 are open, so path 2 is active. One active path is enough: x_2 \not\perp x_3 \mid \{x_1,x_6\}, and the reason is the same collider-opened-by-a-shaded-descendant pattern as Figure 3(a).

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
section: Naive Bayes as a graphical model
text:
Naive Bayes as a graphical model
The tutorial applies Directed graphical models and Conditional independence: three canonical structures to a concrete problem: classifying a text as spam (C=1) or not (C=0) from which words it contains. Represent a text with a bag-of-words vector X = (X_1,\dots,X_d), one binary entry per dictionary word, where X_i=1 means word i appears (order and repetition are discarded). We want the posterior p(C\mid X), and since p(X) does not depend on C, this is proportional to p(C,X).
Applying the chain rule of Why factor the joint with no independence assumptions, in the order C, X_1,\dots,X_d, gives p(C,X) = p(C)\,p(X_1\mid C)\prod_{i=2}^d p(X_i \mid X_1,\dots,X_{i-1}, C). As a DAG this is fully connected: node X_i has i parents, so its CPT alone needs 2^i parameters, and the total is 1 + \sum_{i=1}^d 2^i = 2^{d+1}-1, exactly the general joint-distribution cost from Why factor the joint on d+1 binary variables. Writing the chain rule down bought nothing yet, because no independence was assumed.






Note



Homework-relevant. The next step, the Naive Bayes independence assumption, is where the parameter count collapses, and its MLE derivation is a direct extension of Week 1’s Bernoulli MLE (Maximum likelihood estimation). If a current or upcoming assignment touches maximum likelihood for a probabilistic model, this derivation pattern (Bernoulli log-likelihood, set derivative to zero, read off an empirical frequency) is worth understanding in full rather than only recognizing.


The assumption. Naive Bayes removes every edge between the X_i’s and keeps only the edges from C: p(X_i \mid X_1,\dots,X_{i-1}, C) = p(X_i \mid C), i.e. X_i \perp X_j \mid C for every j \neq i. This is an instance of the common-cause structure from Conditional independence: three canonical structures, with C as the shared cause of every word’s appearance. The factorization becomes p(X,C) = p(C)\prod_{i=1}^d p(X_i \mid C), with 1 + 2d parameters: linear in d instead of exponential. The assumption is not literally true (word co-occurrences do carry information about topic), but it is a Week-1-style parametric simplification: it trades some accuracy in the model for a tractable number of parameters to estimate.
Maximum likelihood. Parameterize p(C{=}1) = \pi and p(X_j{=}1\mid C{=}c) = \theta_{jc}. Given N i.i.d. labelled texts (x^{(i)}, c^{(i)}), the log-likelihood factors, by the same independence assumption, into a sum of Bernoulli log-likelihoods: one for the labels (governed by \pi) and one per word per class (governed by \theta_{jc}): \ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \log p(c^{(i)}) \;+\; \sum_{j=1}^d \sum_{i=1}^N \log p(x_j^{(i)} \mid c^{(i)}). Each piece is a Bernoulli log-likelihood of exactly the shape solved in Week 1 (Maximum likelihood estimation): p(c^{(i)}) = \pi^{c^{(i)}}(1-\pi)^{1-c^{(i)}} and p(x_j^{(i)}\mid c) = \theta_{jc}^{x_j^{(i)}}(1-\theta_{jc})^{1-x_j^{(i)}}. Setting each derivative to zero reproduces the Week 1 pattern, \hat\theta_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i x^{(i)}, applied separately to each piece: \hat\pi = \frac{\sum_i \mathbb{1}[c^{(i)}=1]}{N} = \frac{\#\text{ spam texts}}{\#\text{ texts}}, \hat\theta_{jc} = \frac{\sum_i \mathbb{1}[x_j^{(i)}=1 \,\&\, c^{(i)}=c]}{\sum_i \mathbb{1}[c^{(i)}=c]}. In words, \hat\theta_{jc} is the fraction of class-c texts in which word j appears. Each MLE is again an observed relative frequency, exactly as in the Bernoulli case: the independence assumption did not change how we estimate parameters, only how many there are to estimate.

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
DGMs in the wild, briefly
The tutorial surveys a few more graphical models to show the same “assume some independencies, save parameters” idea recurring in different shapes. None of these are derived in depth in this lecture; the point is to recognize the pattern.

Markov chains. A first-order chain p(x_{1:T}) = p(x_1)\prod_{t=2}^T p(x_t\mid x_{t-1}) assumes each state depends only on the immediately previous one; a second-order chain conditions on the two previous states instead.
Hidden Markov models (HMMs). A chain of unobserved (hidden) states Z_t, each taking one of K discrete values, each emitting an observed X_t: p(X_{1:T}, Z_{1:T}) = p(Z_1)\prod_{t=2}^T p(Z_t\mid Z_{t-1}) \prod_{t=1}^T p(X_t\mid Z_t). This is a Markov chain over the hidden layer, with an emission model attached to each step.
Medical diagnosis networks. The Quick Medical Reference network is a bipartite DAG: hidden disease nodes as parents, observed symptom nodes as children, with a noisy-OR conditional probability table (any positive parent disease tends to make a symptom positive). The Alarm network is a hand-built DAG of 37 ICU-monitoring variables; because it is sparse, it needs only 509 parameters (the tutorial quotes 504), against far more than 2^{37}-1 for a full joint table, since most of its variables have three or four states, and its edges are drawn from known causal relationships in medicine rather than fit as a generic template.

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
Summary






Note



Key takeaways from Week 2:

Decision theory separates inference (estimating p(x,c)) from decision (acting on it). Minimizing misclassification rate is the special case of minimizing expected loss where every error costs the same.
The general discriminant rule minimizes \sum_k L_{kj}\,p(\mathcal{C}_k\mid x) over the decision j; the reject option lets us decline to decide when no posterior clears a threshold.
For regression under squared loss, the best predictor is the conditional expectation y(x) = \mathbb{E}[t\mid x].
A general joint over N binary variables costs 2^N-1 parameters. Directed graphical models trade that cost down by assuming each variable depends only on its parents.
Three structures (chain, common cause, common effect) cover how conditioning opens or blocks dependence; the Bayes Ball algorithm reads x_A\perp x_B\mid x_C directly off the graph using these rules.
Naive Bayes is a common-cause DAG over word features given the class label; its independence assumption is what makes its MLE reduce to per-word, per-class Bernoulli MLEs, in the same shape as Week 1’s Bernoulli derivation.

title: Week 2: Decision Theory and Graphical Models
text:
Quick self-check
If you can explain, in your own words, why the discriminant rule and the best regressor \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] are really the same idea applied to two different loss functions, and why the Naive Bayes assumption is a special case of the “common cause” independence structure, you have understood the core of Week 2.

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
text:
Problem 1: Two ways to be wrong
Overview. These problems drill Week 2. Try each stem before opening the worked solution. The loss matrices, distributions, and graphs here are invented for practice; they are not the cancer-screening, regression, or Bayes-Ball examples from the lecture. Notation matches the week chapter. The exception is the final section, Tutorial questions, which restates the Week 2 tutorial’s own examples.
A helpdesk routes each incoming ticket either to an autoresponder (for routine questions) or to a human agent (for anything else). Two people disagree about how to design the router:
Which objective from the lecture, misclassification rate or expected loss, matches each person’s goal? Could the two objectives ever recommend the same decision rule?
crumbs: 5  Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
text:
Person A wants to minimize the fraction of tickets sent to the wrong handler.
Person B points out that sending a genuinely urgent ticket to the autoresponder is much worse than sending a routine ticket to a human (wasted agent time, but no harm done), and wants the router to reflect that.








TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, From inference to decision and Misclassification rate.
Person A wants to minimize p(\text{mistake}), the plain count of wrong handler assignments from Misclassification rate: every error counts as one, regardless of which direction it runs. Person B wants a loss function (Week 2, Expected loss): a loss matrix that charges more for “urgent ticket sent to autoresponder” than for “routine ticket sent to a human,” and then minimizes the resulting expected loss.
The two objectives can agree. Misclassification rate is the special case of expected loss where the loss matrix has 0 on the diagonal and 1 everywhere off it, so if Person B’s matrix happened to be symmetric with equal off-diagonal costs, the discriminant rule would reduce to Person A’s rule exactly. They diverge only once the loss matrix is asymmetric, which is what Person B is actually asking for.
Answer. Person A: misclassification rate. Person B: expected loss with an asymmetric loss matrix. The two agree whenever the loss matrix has zero diagonal and equal off-diagonal costs (the 0/1 matrix or any positive multiple of it); a loss matrix is a strict generalization, not a different framework.
crumbs: 5  Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
section: Problem 2: Inspecting a batch of widgets
text:
Problem 2: Inspecting a batch of widgets
A factory’s inspection station decides whether a widget is defective (\mathcal{C}_1) or good (\mathcal{C}_2). Passing a defective widget into a shipment costs 50 (recalls, refunds); scrapping a good widget costs 5 (wasted material). Correct calls cost 0.
For one widget, the classifier’s estimated posteriors are p(\mathcal{C}_1 \mid x) = 0.15 and p(\mathcal{C}_2 \mid x) = 0.85.

Write the 2\times 2 loss matrix (rows: truth, columns: decision).
Compute the discriminant rule’s two candidate costs and state its decision.
Compare this to what the misclassification-rate rule (from Problem 1’s Person A) would decide.







TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, Expected loss and The discriminant rule.
1. Loss matrix. L_{\text{defective},\text{scrap}} = 0, L_{\text{defective},\text{ship}} = 50, L_{\text{good},\text{scrap}} = 5, L_{\text{good},\text{ship}} = 0.
2. Discriminant rule. The rule assigns x to the decision j minimizing \sum_k L_{kj}\,p(\mathcal{C}_k\mid x):
\text{cost(ship)} = L_{\text{defective},\text{ship}}(0.15) + L_{\text{good},\text{ship}}(0.85) = 50(0.15) + 0(0.85) = 7.5, \text{cost(scrap)} = L_{\text{defective},\text{scrap}}(0.15) + L_{\text{good},\text{scrap}}(0.85) = 0(0.15) + 5(0.85) = 4.25.
Scrapping is cheaper, so the discriminant rule decides scrap, even though the widget is more likely good (0.85 > 0.15) than defective.
3. Comparison. The plain misclassification-rate rule from Misclassification rate only compares posteriors and would decide ship, since p(\mathcal{C}_2\mid x)=0.85 is the larger posterior. The rules disagree because the loss matrix charges 10 times more for shipping a defective widget than for scrapping a good one, so even a fairly low probability of defect is still worth acting on, exactly the same asymmetry that moved the lecture’s cancer-screening boundary.
Answer. Loss matrix as above; discriminant rule decides scrap (cost 4.25 vs. 7.5); the misclassification-rate rule would have decided ship.
crumbs: 5  Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
text:
Problem 3: A different conditional distribution
Fix an input x. Given that x, a continuous target t takes the values 1, 3, and 14, each with probability \tfrac13.
Compute \mathbb{E}[t\mid x]. Then compare the expected squared loss of the predictor y(x) = 8 against y(x) = \mathbb{E}[t\mid x], and confirm which one the lecture’s theorem says must be smaller.






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, Loss functions for regression.
Conditional mean: \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] = \tfrac13(1+3+14) = 6.
For y(x) = 8: \mathbb{E}[L] = \tfrac13\big[(8-1)^2+(8-3)^2+(8-14)^2\big] = \tfrac13(49+25+36) = \tfrac{110}{3} \approx 36.67.
For y(x) = \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] = 6: \mathbb{E}[L] = \tfrac13\big[(6-1)^2+(6-3)^2+(6-14)^2\big] = \tfrac13(25+9+64) = \tfrac{98}{3} \approx 32.67.
The conditional mean gives the smaller expected loss, matching the theorem: y(x) = \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] minimizes squared loss for any competing choice, not only y(x)=8. The decomposition behind this splits \mathbb{E}[L] into a piece that depends on y(x) (driven to zero exactly at the conditional mean) and a piece that does not (the irreducible noise), so no other constant can do better.
Answer. \mathbb{E}[t\mid x] = 6. Expected loss at y=8 is 110/3 \approx 36.67; at y=6 it is 98/3 \approx 32.67, confirming the conditional mean wins.

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
section: Problem 4: Counting parameters for five variables
text:
Problem 4: Counting parameters for five variables
Take N=5 binary variables x_1,\dots,x_5. Using the chain rule in the order x_1,\dots,x_5 with no assumptions, how many parameters does the factorization need?
Now suppose we are willing to assume x_5 depends only on x_2 and x_4 (not on x_1 or x_3), while every other factor stays as general as before. How many parameters does the factorization need now, and how many were saved?






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, Free parameters and the cost of the full joint and Why factor the joint.
With no assumptions, the chain rule gives p(x_1)p(x_2\mid x_1)p(x_3\mid x_1,x_2)p(x_4\mid x_1,x_2,x_3)p(x_5\mid x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4). Each factor p(x_j\mid x_1,\dots,x_{j-1}) needs 2^{j-1} parameters, so the totals are 1,2,4,8,16 for j=1,\dots,5, summing to 1+2+4+8+16=31, matching 2^5-1=31 exactly.
Replacing the last factor with p(x_5\mid x_2,x_4) shrinks its table from 2^4=16 parameters (one per configuration of four parents) to 2^2=4 (one per configuration of two parents). The new total is 1+2+4+8+4 = 19.
Savings: 31-19=12 parameters, all from dropping x_5’s dependence on x_1 and x_3. This is the same pattern as the lecture’s N=4 example: dropping dependence on conditioning variables shrinks that one factor’s table exponentially, and the saving compounds because that factor was the largest one in the sum.
Answer. No assumptions: 31 parameters. With x_5\mid x_2,x_4: 19 parameters. Savings: 12.

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
section: Problem 5: CPT sizes for an invented graph
text:
Problem 5: CPT sizes for an invented graph
Consider a DAG on five binary nodes y_1,\dots,y_5 with edges y_1 \to y_2, y_1 \to y_3, y_2 \to y_4, y_3 \to y_4, y_4 \to y_5 (so y_4 has two parents, y_2 and y_3).
For each node, state its parent count K_i and its CPT size 2^{K_i}. Sum these to get the total number of parameters, and compare to the 2^5-1 a fully-connected DAG on five nodes would need.






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, Directed graphical models.
Read the parent count off the incoming edges at each node:

y_1: no parents, K=0, CPT size 2^0=1.
y_2: one parent (y_1), K=1, CPT size 2^1=2.
y_3: one parent (y_1), K=1, CPT size 2.
y_4: two parents (y_2,y_3), K=2, CPT size 2^2=4.
y_5: one parent (y_4), K=1, CPT size 2.

Total: 1+2+2+4+2 = 11 parameters, against 2^5-1=31 for the fully-connected case on five nodes. The saving comes from every node having at most two parents instead of depending on every node before it; y_4’s CPT is the largest single piece because it is the only node with two parents.
Answer. K = (0,1,1,2,1), CPT sizes (1,2,2,4,2), total 11 parameters, versus 31 fully connected.

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
section: Problem 6: Chain, common cause, or collider?
text:
Problem 6: Chain, common cause, or collider?
Three sensors on a machine: a temperature reading (X), an internal wear level (Y), and a vibration reading (Z). Consider this causal story: high internal wear (Y) tends to raise both the temperature reading (X) and the vibration reading (Z), but the temperature and vibration sensors do not affect each other directly: X \leftarrow Y \rightarrow Z.
Which of the lecture’s three canonical structures is this? Are X and Z independent before observing Y? What happens once Y (the wear level) is observed?






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, Conditional independence: three canonical structures.
This is the common cause structure, X \leftarrow Y \rightarrow Z, with wear level Y as the shared cause of both readings.
Marginally (before observing Y), X and Z are dependent: a high temperature reading is evidence of high wear, which in turn makes a high vibration reading more likely, so the two readings move together even though neither sensor affects the other. This is the same “two effects of a shared cause are correlated” pattern as the lecture’s deadline example.
Once Y is observed, the joint factors as p(y)p(x\mid y)p(z\mid y), so p(x,z\mid y) = p(x\mid y)p(z\mid y): conditioning on the wear level uses up the shared explanation, and X \perp Z \mid Y. Knowing the wear level directly, the temperature reading tells us nothing more about the vibration reading.
Answer. Common cause. X and Z are marginally dependent, and become conditionally independent given Y: X \perp Z \mid Y.
crumbs: 5  Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
section: Problem 7: Bayes Ball on a small graph
text:
Problem 7: Bayes Ball on a small graph
Consider a DAG with edges p \to q, r \to q, q \to s, r \to t (so q is a collider with parents p and r, and r also has a second child t).

Is p \perp r \mid \emptyset (no conditioning set)?
Is p \perp r \mid \{s\}?
Is p \perp t \mid \{r\}?

For each, name the only path between the two nodes, identify the junction type(s) on it, and apply the Bayes Ball rules.






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, The Bayes Ball algorithm.
1. p \perp r \mid \emptyset. The only path between p and r is p \to q \leftarrow r. Here q is a collider. With C=\emptyset, neither q nor any descendant of q (that is, s) is in C, so the collider is blocked. The one path is blocked, so p \perp r \mid \emptyset.
2. p \perp r \mid \{s\}. Same path, p \to q \leftarrow r, same collider q. Now C=\{s\}, and s is a descendant of the collider q (via q \to s), so the collider is open: shading a descendant of a collider opens it, exactly the explaining-away rule. The path is active, so p \not\perp r \mid \{s\}. Conditioning on s, which is not even on the direct route between p and r, is what creates the dependency, the same pattern as the lecture’s c-shaded example.
3. p \perp t \mid \{r\}. The only path between p and t is p \to q \leftarrow r \to t. There are two junctions: q is a collider (parents p,r), and r is a fork on this path (edges r\to q and r\to t both point out of r). With C=\{r\}: at the fork r, r is shaded, so the fork is blocked. That already blocks the whole path regardless of q (checking anyway: at the collider q, neither q nor its descendant s is in C=\{r\}, so q is also blocked). So p \perp t \mid \{r\}.
Answer. (1) p\perp r\mid\emptyset: yes. (2) p\perp r\mid\{s\}: no. (3) p\perp t\mid\{r\}: yes.
crumbs: 5  Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
section: Problem 8: Why does Naive Bayes save so many parameters?
text:
Problem 8: Why does Naive Bayes save so many parameters?
A grocer wants to classify fruit as ripe (C=1) or unripe (C=0) from three binary features: color (X_1: red/green), softness (X_2: soft/firm), and smell (X_3: fragrant/faint). A Naive Bayes model assumes X_1, X_2, X_3 are conditionally independent given the ripeness label C.
Without computing any specific numbers, explain: (a) which of the lecture’s three canonical structures this independence assumption corresponds to, and why; (b) in general terms, why the assumption shrinks the parameter count from exponential in the number of features to linear in the number of features. (The exact MLE formulas for \hat\pi and \hat\theta_{jc} are left to work through with real counts on your own data; this problem is about the structural reason for the saving, not the computed values.)






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, Naive Bayes as a graphical model and Directed graphical models.
(a) Which structure. The assumption X_i \perp X_j \mid C for every feature pair is the common-cause structure repeated across every pair of features, with the ripeness label C playing the role of the shared cause. Each feature is an effect of C (color, softness, and smell are all downstream of whether the fruit is actually ripe), and once C is known, no feature carries extra information about any other feature. This is exactly the deadline example and Problem 6’s sensor example, generalized from one shared cause and two effects to one shared cause and d effects.
(b) Why the parameter count shrinks. Without any independence assumption, the DAG on C, X_1, X_2, X_3 is fully connected in the chain-rule order C,X_1,X_2,X_3: the i-th feature’s CPT conditions on C and every feature before it, so its table size doubles with each additional feature, giving a total that grows as 2^{d+1}-1 in the number of features d (Free parameters and the cost of the full joint, Why factor the joint). Removing every edge between features and keeping only the edges from C means each feature’s CPT now conditions on C alone, a table of fixed size regardless of how many other features exist. Summing a fixed-size table once per feature gives a total that grows linearly in d instead of exponentially. The structural reason is the same one from Directed graphical models: restricting how many parents a node can have is what buys the saving, and Naive Bayes pushes every feature’s parent set down to just \{C\}, the most aggressive restriction available short of assuming no dependence on C at all.
Answer. (a) Common cause, with C as the shared parent of every feature. (b) Fully connected costs grow exponentially in the number of features because each new feature’s CPT can condition on every earlier feature; capping every feature’s parent set at \{C\} makes each CPT a fixed size, so the total grows linearly instead.

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
text:
Conditional independence drills
These problems drill conditional independence from both sides: checking it numerically from a table, and reading it off a graph. All setups are invented.

Problem 9: Independent given C, dependent without it
Three binary variables A,B,C have the joint distribution



(a,b,c)

0.03
0.07

0.01




Check that A\perp B\mid C for C=1: is p(A{=}1,B{=}1\mid C{=}1)=p(A{=}1\mid C{=}1)\,p(B{=}1\mid C{=}1)? (The other entries and C=0 work the same way.)
Are A and B independent marginally?







TipWorked solution





This uses the definition in Week 2, Conditional independence: three canonical structures, together with Week 1’s sum rule.

First p(C{=}1)=0.03+0.07+0.12+0.28=0.5. Then p(A{=}1\mid C{=}1)=\frac{0.12+0.28}{0.5}=0.8, \qquad p(B{=}1\mid C{=}1)=\frac{0.07+0.28}{0.5}=0.7, p(A{=}1,B{=}1\mid C{=}1)=\frac{0.28}{0.5}=0.56=0.8\times0.7. The product rule holds. Doing the same for C=0 gives 0.02=0.2\times0.1, so A\perp B\mid C.
Sum out C: p(A{=}1)=0.12+0.28+0.09+0.01=0.5, p(B{=}1)=0.07+0.28+0.04+0.01=0.4, and p(A{=}1,B{=}1)=0.28+0.01=0.29. Since 0.29\neq0.5\times0.4=0.20, A and B are dependent.

C is a common cause: it makes both A and B likely to be 1 together. Once C is known it explains everything they share, but if C is summed out, seeing A{=}1 hints that C{=}1, which makes B{=}1 more likely.
Answer. (1) Yes, 0.56=0.8\times0.7. (2) No: p(A{=}1,B{=}1)=0.29\neq0.20.





Problem 10: Why the three definitions agree
The week chapter gives three equivalent ways to say A\perp B\mid C. Show that p(a\mid b,c)=p(a\mid c) implies p(a,b\mid c)=p(a\mid c)\,p(b\mid c), and then show the reverse (assuming p(b\mid c)>0).






TipWorked solution





This proves the equivalence stated in the definition of Week 2, Conditional independence: three canonical structures. The only tool is the product rule with everything conditioned on c: p(a,b\mid c)=p(a\mid b,c)\,p(b\mid c).
Forward. Substitute p(a\mid b,c)=p(a\mid c) into the product rule: p(a,b\mid c)=p(a\mid c)\,p(b\mid c).
Reverse. Rearrange the product rule and substitute the factorization: p(a\mid b,c)=\frac{p(a,b\mid c)}{p(b\mid c)}=\frac{p(a\mid c)\,p(b\mid c)}{p(b\mid c)}=p(a\mid c).
The third form, p(b\mid a,c)=p(b\mid c), follows the same way with a and b swapped. All three say “once c is known, learning one of a,b tells us nothing more about the other”.
Answer. Both directions follow from p(a,b\mid c)=p(a\mid b,c)\,p(b\mid c).





Problem 11: Explaining away with two coins
Flip two independent fair coins, X and Z (1 for heads), and let Y=1 if at least one of them is heads, Y=0 otherwise. Compute p(Z{=}1), p(Z{=}1\mid Y{=}1), and p(Z{=}1\mid Y{=}1,X{=}1). What does this say about X and Z once Y is observed?






TipWorked solution





This is the explaining-away structure of Week 2, Conditional independence: three canonical structures, with Y a collider: X\to Y\leftarrow Z.

p(Z{=}1)=\frac12.
Y=1 in three of the four equally likely outcomes (HT,TH,HH), and Z=1 in two of them, so p(Z{=}1\mid Y{=}1)=\frac{2/4}{3/4}=\frac23.
If also X=1, then Y=1 is already guaranteed, so it carries no information about Z: p(Z{=}1\mid Y{=}1,X{=}1)=p(Z{=}1)=\frac12.

Given Y=1, learning X=1 moves our belief about Z from \frac23 down to \frac12: X=1 has “explained away” why Y=1. So X and Z, independent to begin with, are dependent once their common effect is observed.
Answer. \frac12, \frac23, \frac12: X\perp Z but X\not\perp Z\mid Y.





Problem 12: Which statements hold in a chain?
In the first-order chain X_1\to X_2\to X_3\to X_4, mark each statement as always true or not true in general:

X_1\perp X_3\mid X_2
X_1\perp X_4\mid X_2
X_1\perp X_4\mid X_3
X_1\perp X_3
X_2\perp X_4\mid X_1







TipWorked solution





This uses the chain structure of Week 2, Conditional independence: three canonical structures and the blocking rule of Week 2, The Bayes Ball algorithm. There is only one path between any two nodes, and every interior node on it is a chain node, so a path is blocked exactly when some node strictly between the endpoints is observed.

The path X_1\to X_2\to X_3 passes through the observed X_2: blocked. True.
The path X_1\to X_2\to X_3\to X_4 passes through the observed X_2: blocked. True.
The same path passes through the observed X_3: blocked. True.
Nothing is observed, so the path is open. Not true in general.
The path X_2\to X_3\to X_4 does not pass through X_1, so observing X_1 does not block it. Not true in general.

Answer. 1, 2, 3 true; 4 and 5 not true in general.





Problem 13: d-separation on a new graph
A DAG has edges u\to v, w\to v, v\to x, w\to y, y\to z. Decide each of the following:

u\perp w
u\perp w\mid x
u\perp y\mid x
u\perp z\mid\{x,y\}







TipWorked solution





This applies the d-separation definition of Week 2, The Bayes Ball algorithm. Every path from u must go u\to v\leftarrow w, so v is always a collider on it; its only descendant is x. From w the path can continue w\to y\to z, where w is a fork and y is a chain node.

Path u\to v\leftarrow w. Neither v nor x is observed, so the collider blocks. Independent.
Now x, a descendant of v, is observed, so the collider is open. The path is active: not independent.
Path u\to v\leftarrow w\to y. The collider v is open (via x), and the fork w is unobserved, so it is open too. Active: not independent.
Path u\to v\leftarrow w\to y\to z. The collider is open, but the chain node y is observed, which blocks it. This is the only path, so independent.

Answer. (1) Yes. (2) No. (3) No. (4) Yes.

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
text:
Tutorial questions
The questions below are the Week 2 tutorial’s examples, restated as questions. They use the tutorial’s own graphs and models, so several are also worked in the week chapter; each solution says where.

Tutorial question 1: Factorize the Bayes Ball graph
A DAG has five nodes with edges a\to e, f\to e, e\to c, and f\to b (the graph of Week 2, Figure 3). Ignoring any observed nodes, what factorization of p(a,b,c,e,f) does it imply?






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, Directed graphical models: one factor per node, conditioned on that node’s parents. a and f have no parents, e has parents a and f, c has parent e, and b has parent f.
Answer. p(a,b,c,e,f)=p(a)\,p(f)\,p(e\mid a,f)\,p(c\mid e)\,p(b\mid f).





Tutorial question 2: Is a independent of b?
On the same graph, use Bayes Ball to decide whether a\perp b:

conditioned on c;
conditioned on f.







TipWorked solution





This is the tutorial example worked in Week 2, The Bayes Ball algorithm.
The only path from a to b is a\to e\leftarrow f\to b. It has two interior nodes: e, where the arrows meet head-to-head, and f, where they meet tail-to-tail.

Conditioning on c: e is a collider that is not observed, but its descendant c is, so rule (b) does not block it. f is tail-to-tail and not observed, so rule (a) does not block it either. The path is open.
Conditioning on f: f is tail-to-tail and observed, which blocks the path by rule (a). (e is also blocking, since neither it nor its descendant c is observed.)

Answer. (a) No, a\not\perp b\mid c. (b) Yes, a\perp b\mid f.





Tutorial question 3: The general spam model
A text is classified as spam (C=1) or not (C=0) from a bag-of-words vector X=(X_1,\dots,X_d), where X_i\in\{0,1\} records whether dictionary word i appears. Without any independence assumptions, factorize p(C,X) with the chain rule in the order C,X_1,\dots,X_d. Draw the corresponding DAG in your head: how many edges enter X_i, and how many parameters does the whole model need?






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, Free parameters and the cost of the full joint and Week 2, Naive Bayes as a graphical model.
The chain rule gives p(C,X)=p(C)\,p(X_1\mid C)\prod_{i=2}^dp(X_i\mid X_1,\dots,X_{i-1},C). Each factor conditions on everything to its left, so the DAG has an edge into each node from every earlier node. The graph on d+1 nodes is fully connected.
Node X_i has i parents (C and X_1,\dots,X_{i-1}), all binary, so its table has 2^i rows, each needing one number. C needs 1 number. The total is 1+\sum_{i=1}^d2^i=1+(2^{d+1}-2)=2^{d+1}-1, the same as specifying the full joint table over d+1 binary variables. This factorization assumes nothing, so it saves nothing.
Answer. X_i has i incoming edges; the model needs 2^{d+1}-1 parameters.





Tutorial question 4: Naive Bayes
Now remove every edge between the X_i’s and keep only the edges from C. What factorization does this imply, what independence does it assume, and how many parameters does it need?






TipWorked solution





This is Week 2, Naive Bayes as a graphical model.
Each X_i now has the single parent C, so p(C,X)=p(C)\prod_{i=1}^dp(X_i\mid C). The assumption is p(X_i\mid X_1,\dots,X_{i-1},C)=p(X_i\mid C): every word is independent of every other word given the class. C needs 1 parameter and each X_i needs 2 (one for each value of C).
Answer. p(C)\prod_ip(X_i\mid C), with 1+2d parameters: linear in d instead of exponential.





Tutorial question 5: Learning Naive Bayes by maximum likelihood
Parameterize the Naive Bayes model by p(C=1)=\pi and p(X_j=1\mid C=c)=\theta_{jc}. Given N labelled texts (x^{(i)},c^{(i)}), write the log-likelihood as a sum of Bernoulli log-likelihoods and find the MLEs of \pi and \theta_{jc}.






TipWorked solution





This reteaches Week 2, Naive Bayes as a graphical model using the Bernoulli MLE of Week 1, Maximum likelihood estimation.
Split the log-likelihood. The factorization turns the log of each example’s probability into a sum: \ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^N\log p(c^{(i)})+\sum_{j=1}^d\sum_{i=1}^N\log p\big(x_j^{(i)}\mid c^{(i)}\big). The first sum involves only \pi; the j-th inner sum involves only \theta_{j0} and \theta_{j1}. Each piece can be maximized separately.
The labels. p(c^{(i)})=\pi^{c^{(i)}}(1-\pi)^{1-c^{(i)}}, so the first sum is \sum_ic^{(i)}\log\pi+\sum_i(1-c^{(i)})\log(1-\pi), a Bernoulli log-likelihood.
The features. p(x_j^{(i)}\mid c)=\theta_{jc}^{x_j^{(i)}}(1-\theta_{jc})^{1-x_j^{(i)}}. Splitting the examples by label, the j-th sum is a Bernoulli log-likelihood for \theta_{j1} over the spam texts plus one for \theta_{j0} over the others.
Set derivatives to zero. Each Bernoulli MLE is a fraction of ones: \hat\pi=\frac{\sum_i\mathbb{1}[c^{(i)}=1]}{N}, \qquad \hat\theta_{jc}=\frac{\sum_i\mathbb{1}[x_j^{(i)}=1,\ c^{(i)}=c]}{\sum_i\mathbb{1}[c^{(i)}=c]}.
Answer. \hat\pi is the fraction of texts that are spam; \hat\theta_{j1} is the fraction of spam texts containing word j (and \hat\theta_{j0} the same among non-spam texts).





Tutorial question 6: A second-order Markov chain
The order of a Markov chain is the number of previous states the current state may depend on. Write the factorization of p(x_{1:T}) for a first-order chain and for a second-order chain. Which edges does the second-order DAG add?






TipWorked solution





This expands the Markov-chain bullet of Week 2, DGMs in the wild. Week 5 develops Markov chains in full.
First order, each state depends on the one before: p(x_{1:T})=p(x_1)\prod_{t=2}^Tp(x_t\mid x_{t-1}). Second order, each state depends on the two before: p(x_{1:T})=p(x_1,x_2)\prod_{t=3}^Tp(x_t\mid x_{t-1},x_{t-2}). The first two states have no two predecessors, so they share the opening factor p(x_1,x_2).
Answer. The second-order DAG keeps the edges x_{t-1}\to x_t and adds a skip edge x_{t-2}\to x_t into every node from x_3 on.





Tutorial question 7: Hidden Markov models
In a hidden Markov model, hidden states Z_t (each taking one of K values) form a first-order Markov chain, and each Z_t emits an observation X_t. Write the factorization of p(X_{1:T},Z_{1:T}).






TipWorked solution





This is the HMM bullet of Week 2, DGMs in the wild. Write the joint as p(Z_{1:T})\,p(X_{1:T}\mid Z_{1:T}). The first factor is a first-order chain. In the second, each X_t has the single parent Z_t.
Answer. p(X_{1:T},Z_{1:T})=p(Z_1)\prod_{t=2}^Tp(Z_t\mid Z_{t-1})\prod_{t=1}^Tp(X_t\mid Z_t).





Tutorial question 8: The noisy-OR model
The Quick Medical Reference network has binary hidden disease nodes h=\{h_s\} and binary visible symptom nodes v=\{v_t\}, with edges only from diseases to symptoms. Its symptom model is a noisy-OR: p(v_t=0\mid h)=\prod_{s\in\mathrm{pa}(t)}\theta_{st}^{\mathbb{1}(h_s=1)}, \qquad \theta_{st}=p(v_t=0\mid h_s=1,\ \text{all other parents }0).

Write the joint p(v,h) and give p(v_t=1\mid h).
Without any extra node, what is p(v_t=1\mid h) for a patient with none of the listed diseases? Why does the model add a dummy disease h_0 that is always 1?







TipWorked solution





This expands the medical-diagnosis bullet of Week 2, DGMs in the wild.

Diseases have no parents and each symptom’s parents are diseases, so p(v,h)=\prod_sp(h_s)\prod_tp\big(v_t\mid h_{\mathrm{pa}(t)}\big), \qquad p(v_t=1\mid h)=1-\prod_{s\in\mathrm{pa}(t)}\theta_{st}^{\mathbb{1}(h_s=1)}. The tutorial’s reading: flip one coin per active parent disease, with heads probability \theta_{st}. The symptom is absent only if every coin comes up heads.
With no active disease every exponent is 0, the product is 1, and p(v_t=1\mid h)=0: such a patient could never show any symptom, so observing a symptom with no listed cause would get probability zero. The dummy node h_0=1 stands for all unknown diseases. It is always active, so it contributes a factor \theta_{0t} to every product.

Answer. (1) p(v_t=1\mid h)=1-\prod_{s}\theta_{st}^{\mathbb{1}(h_s=1)}. (2) Zero without the dummy node; with it, 1-\theta_{0t}>0.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
text:
From DAGs to undirected graphs
Overview. Week 2 built directed graphical models: pick an ordering of the variables, draw an arrow from each parent to each child, and read conditional independencies off the arrows. That works well when there is a natural causal or generative ordering, but many domains (a social network, a protein interaction network, the pixels of an image) have no natural direction to assign to an edge. This lecture introduces Markov random fields (MRFs), undirected graphical models where an edge means “these two variables interact” rather than “one causes the other.” We show what MRFs can express that DAGs cannot, and vice versa, then specialize to two concrete families: the Ising model (for discrete/binary variables) and Gaussian graphical models (for continuous ones), the latter directly useful for this course’s first assignment. The second half turns to exact inference: given a graphical model, how do we actually compute a marginal or conditional probability without enumerating every possible assignment? Variable elimination answers this for both DAGs and MRFs at once, and we finish with a worked example and a modern application, the restricted Boltzmann machine.
Skipped: the title slide and the assignment/office-hours announcements on slide 2 (the content summary from that same slide becomes the paragraph above).
Week 2 represented a joint distribution with a DAG, where every edge has a direction. Some problems have no natural direction: neighbouring pixels in an image, for example, influence each other symmetrically. To see what directed edges cost us in such a problem, we look at how much of the graph a single variable depends on, which is measured by its Markov blanket.
Recall the Markov blanket of a variable X_i: the smallest set of other variables that makes X_i conditionally independent of everything else. In a DAG, the Markov blanket of X_i is its parents, its children, and its children’s other parents (the co-parents), because of the explaining-away effect from Week 2 (Conditional independence: three canonical structures in Week 2): observing a child can create dependence between that child’s parents.
This has an awkward consequence. Take a grid of variables X_1,\dots,X_{20} arranged in rows, where intuitively each variable should depend only on its four grid neighbors (up, down, left, right). If we try to encode this as a DAG by choosing some ordering of the variables (say, left to right, top to bottom) and drawing arrows accordingly, the Markov blanket of an interior node like X_8 can end up including nodes that have nothing to do with X_8’s grid neighbors. Figure 1 shows the lecture’s version: every horizontal edge points right and every vertical edge points down.
Reading X_8’s Markov blanket off Figure 1 with the parents, children, co-parents rule:
The first two groups are exactly X_8’s four grid neighbors, as we would expect. X_4 and X_{12} are the surprise: they sit diagonally from X_8 and share no edge with it. They are in the blanket because of the co-parent rule, which comes from the collider case of Week 2’s d-separation rule (The Bayes Ball algorithm in Week 2). The path X_8\to X_9\leftarrow X_4 meets head-to-head at X_9, so X_9 is a collider on it. A Markov blanket must contain X_8’s children, so X_9 is conditioned on. A collider blocks a path only when neither it nor any of its descendants is observed, so an observed collider leaves the path active. This is explaining away: given X_9, learning X_4 changes what we believe about X_8, its other cause. The only way to cut that path is to condition on X_4 too. The same argument through X_{13} puts X_{12} in the blanket.
The asymmetry gives the orientation away. The other two diagonal cells, X_2 and X_{14}, are not in the blanket: X_2’s children are X_3 and X_7, which are parents of X_8 rather than children, and X_{14} is a child of X_9 and X_{13}, not a parent of either. Which diagonals join the blanket depends only on which way the arrows were drawn. The DAG is not wrong: it does encode a valid factorization. But its dependency structure does not match the “each cell depends on its neighbors” structure we actually wanted to express, and no choice of edge directions fixes this in general.
Figure 1. The lecture’s grid as a DAG, with every edge pointing right or down. X_8’s Markov blanket is its parents X_3, X_7 (blue), its children X_9, X_{13} (green), and its co-parents X_4, X_{12} (orange). The highlighted edges X_4\to X_9 and X_{12}\to X_{13} are what make X_4 and X_{12} co-parents, even though neither is a grid neighbor of X_8.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
section: Markov random fields, cliques, and the factorization theorem
text:
Markov random fields, cliques, and the factorization theorem
The grid shows the problem with arrows: they force us to choose directions the problem does not have, and that choice drags non-neighbours like X_4 and X_{12} into X_8’s blanket through colliders. The fix is to drop the arrows. In an undirected graph an edge only says “these two variables interact”, there are no colliders, and (as The Hammersley-Clifford theorem will show) a node’s Markov blanket is just its neighbours. An undirected graph then needs its own rule for which distributions it represents, which is what this section sets up.

Definition. An undirected graphical model, or Markov random field (MRF), represents a set of random variables as nodes of an undirected graph G, where an edge between two nodes means those variables interact directly, rather than one causing the other.

To write down what distributions an MRF represents, we need the notion of a clique.

Definition. A clique is a subset of nodes in which every pair is connected by an edge. A maximal clique is a clique that cannot be extended by adding one more adjacent node without breaking the all-pairs-connected property.


Definition. Let \boldsymbol{x} = (x_1,\dots,x_m) be all the variables in graph G, and let \mathcal{C} be the set of all maximal cliques of G. A distribution p factorizes with respect to G if p(\boldsymbol{x}) \propto \prod_{C \in \mathcal{C}} \psi_C(x_C) for some nonnegative potential functions \psi_C, where x_C = (x_i)_{i \in C}. The MRF on G represents exactly the distributions that factorize with respect to G.







TipQuestion: What does the C in psi_C mean, and are we free to define these functions however we like?





What C stands for. C is a clique: a set of node indices, such as C=\{1,2,3\}. The product \prod_{C\in\mathcal{C}} runs over every maximal clique of the graph, and x_C is the list of values of just the variables in that clique. So \psi_C(x_C) is “the potential attached to clique C, evaluated at that clique’s variables.” In practice we write the clique’s members as the subscript: for C=\{1,2,3\}, \psi_C(x_C) is written \psi_{1,2,3}(x_1,x_2,x_3). The letter \psi (psi) has no meaning of its own; it is the usual name for a potential.
What we may choose. Almost anything, within three rules:

Nonnegative. \psi_C(x_C)\ge 0 for every setting. Hammersley-Clifford (The Hammersley-Clifford theorem) needs the resulting p to be strictly positive, which is why potentials are often written as \psi_C = e^{(\text{something})}, which can never be zero.
Only the clique’s own variables. \psi_{1,2,3} may look at x_1,x_2,x_3 and nothing else. This rule is the entire content of the graph: it is what stops a factor from linking two variables that share no edge.
No normalization. A potential need not sum to 1 and is not a probability. Multiplying one potential by a constant changes nothing once we divide by Z.

Within those rules, choosing the potentials is the modelling step. They are usually given a parametric form and learned from data, such as the Ising model’s \psi_{st}=e^{J_{st}x_sx_t} (The Ising model) or the log-linear form of MRFs as exponential families.
Potentials on smaller cliques. We may also attach potentials to single nodes or to edges inside a larger clique, as the Ising model does with its per-node field. This does not enlarge the family of distributions: any such factor can be multiplied into the potential of a maximal clique that contains it, which recovers the one-potential-per-maximal-clique form above.









TipQuestion: What does it mean for a distribution to factorize with respect to a graph, concretely?





What “factorizes” means. A function of many variables factorizes if it can be written as a product of smaller functions, each of which looks at only some of the variables. Week 2 already did this for DAGs: p(x_1,\dots,x_N)=\prod_ip(x_i\mid\text{parents}(x_i)), where each factor involves one node and its parents (Directed graphical models in Week 2). Here the factors are potentials instead of conditional probabilities, and the graph decides which groups of variables are allowed to share a factor: one factor per maximal clique. “With respect to G” means exactly that restriction. Any distribution can be written as a single factor over all its variables, but that only factorizes with respect to the complete graph.
A concrete example. Take the chain X_1-X_2-X_3 with each X_i\in\{0,1\}. Its maximal cliques are the edges \{1,2\} and \{2,3\}, so a distribution factorizes with respect to this graph if p(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\frac1Z\,\psi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2)\,\psi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3). Choose both potentials to reward agreement, as in the Ising model of The Ising model: \psi(a,b)=2 if a=b and 1 if a\neq b. Multiplying the two potentials for each of the 8 settings gives the unnormalized table:



(x_1,x_2,x_3)

\psi_{1,2}\,\psi_{2,3}

The entries sum to Z=18, so for example p(0,0,0)=4/18=2/9 and p(0,1,0)=1/18. Eight probabilities were specified by two 2\times2 tables: that saving is the point of factorizing.
What the factorization buys. Because no factor contains both x_1 and x_3, they can only influence each other through x_2. Check it with the definition of conditional probability (Bayes’ rule), dividing the joint by the marginal of what we condition on: p(x_3\mid x_1,x_2)=\frac{p(x_1,x_2,x_3)}{p(x_1,x_2)}=\frac{p(x_1,x_2,x_3)}{\sum_{x_3'}p(x_1,x_2,x_3')}. The \frac1Z in every joint probability cancels between numerator and denominator, so the table entries can be used directly. With x_2=0 and x_1=0: p(x_3=0\mid x_1=0,x_2=0)=\frac{p(0,0,0)}{p(0,0,0)+p(0,0,1)}=\frac{4/18}{4/18+2/18}=\frac{4}{4+2}=\frac23. With x_2=0 and x_1=1: p(x_3=0\mid x_1=1,x_2=0)=\frac{p(1,0,0)}{p(1,0,0)+p(1,0,1)}=\frac{2/18}{2/18+1/18}=\frac{2}{2+1}=\frac23. Changing x_1 does not change the answer once x_2 is known, so X_1\perp X_3\mid X_2. This is the independence that The Hammersley-Clifford theorem reads directly off the graph.
A distribution that does not factorize. Let X_2 be a fair coin, independent of everything, and let X_1=X_3 be a second fair coin, so p(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\frac14 when x_1=x_3 and 0 otherwise. Given x_2, knowing x_1 still tells us x_3 exactly, so X_1\not\perp X_3\mid X_2. Every distribution of the form \frac1Z\psi_{1,2}\psi_{2,3} has X_1\perp X_3\mid X_2 (the general proof is the chain argument in The Hammersley-Clifford theorem; the check above is one instance), so no choice of potentials can produce this one. It factorizes only with respect to a graph with an edge between X_1 and X_3.



Unlike a DAG’s conditional probability tables, a potential \psi_C need not sum or integrate to 1, and need not have any probabilistic interpretation on its own; it is simply a nonnegative score attached to each joint setting of the clique’s variables. The product of all the potentials is only proportional to p(\boldsymbol{x}), so an explicit normalizing constant Z = \sum_{\boldsymbol{x}} \prod_{C} \psi_C(x_C) (the partition function) is needed to turn it into an actual probability. This factored structure is what makes sums and integrals over p(\boldsymbol{x}) tractable: instead of manipulating one giant table over all variables jointly, we manipulate several small tables, one per clique, exactly the same motivation that drove the chain-rule factorization of Week 2 (Why factor the joint in Week 2).
As a small concrete instance, a 4-cycle of binary variables x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4 (edges 1\text{-}2, 2\text{-}3, 3\text{-}4, 4\text{-}1) has four maximal cliques, one per edge, so
p(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4) = \frac{1}{Z}\,\psi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2)\,\psi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3)\,\psi_{3,4}(x_3,x_4)\,\psi_{1,4}(x_1,x_4).

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
text:
The Hammersley-Clifford theorem
We now have two ways to read an undirected graph. Markov random fields, cliques, and the factorization theorem reads it as a factorization: a product of clique potentials. The motivation in From DAGs to undirected graphs reads it as a set of independence statements: a variable should depend only on its neighbours. Nothing so far says these two readings describe the same distributions. The Hammersley-Clifford theorem says they do, for distributions that are strictly positive.

Hammersley-Clifford theorem. If p(\boldsymbol{x}) > 0 for all \boldsymbol{x}, the following are equivalent:

p factorizes with respect to G, i.e. p(\boldsymbol{x}) \propto \prod_{C \in \mathcal{C}} \psi_C(x_C) for nonnegative potentials \psi_C.
Global Markov property: X_A \perp X_B \mid X_S whenever S separates A from B in G (every path from A to B passes through S).


Two special cases of the global Markov property are worth naming directly, since they recur constantly: if i and j are not joined by an edge, then X_i \perp X_j \mid X_{\text{rest}} (conditioning on every other variable separates any two non-adjacent nodes); and the Markov blanket of X_i in an MRF is simply its graph neighbors, no co-parent correction needed, in contrast to the DAG case of From DAGs to undirected graphs.
Why the two directions match: a chain. The core mechanism is easiest to see on a three-node chain X-Y-Z, whose only maximal cliques are the edges \{X,Y\} and \{Y,Z\}, so the class of distributions that factorizes with respect to this graph is exactly those of the form f(x,y,z) = \alpha(x,y)\,\beta(y,z) for positive functions \alpha,\beta. The claim is that this is equivalent to X \perp Z \mid Y.
Independent \Rightarrow factorized. Using the product rule, f(x,y,z) = f(y,z)\,f(x\mid y,z), and separately f(x,y,z) = f(x\mid y)\,f(y,z) whenever X\perp Z\mid Y already holds, so a factorization of the stated form is available with \alpha(x,y) = f(x\mid y) and \beta(y,z) = f(y,z). This direction just restates the definition of conditional independence as a factorization.
Factorized \Rightarrow independent, without assuming it first. Start only from f(x,y,z)=\alpha(x,y)\beta(y,z) and derive the independence. Summing out x, f(y,z) = \Big(\sum_x \alpha(x,y)\Big)\beta(y,z). Dividing the joint by this marginal gives the conditional: f(x\mid y,z) = \frac{\alpha(x,y)\,\beta(y,z)}{\left(\sum_x \alpha(x,y)\right)\beta(y,z)} = \frac{\alpha(x,y)}{\sum_x \alpha(x,y)}. The right-hand side has no z in it at all, so f(x\mid y,z) does not depend on z, which is exactly X\perp Z\mid Y. The mechanism is the same cancellation as Week 2’s causal-chain check (Conditional independence: three canonical structures in Week 2): a shared factor in numerator and denominator drops out, leaving no trace of the conditioned-out variable.

Figure 3. A seven-node MRF with edges 1\text{-}2, 1\text{-}3, 2\text{-}3, 2\text{-}4, 2\text{-}5, 3\text{-}5, 3\text{-}6, 4\text{-}5, 4\text{-}6, 4\text{-}7, 5\text{-}6, 5\text{-}7, 6\text{-}7.
How many maximal cliques are there? Checking every pairwise connection within each candidate set gives five maximal cliques: \{1,2,3\}, \{2,3,5\}, \{2,4,5\}, \{3,5,6\}, and \{4,5,6,7\}. Node 5 belongs to four of the five, since it connects to nearly every other node; that is exactly why it appears in so many of the clique’s variable lists below.
What is the factorization? p(\boldsymbol{x}) \propto \psi_{1,2,3}(x_1,x_2,x_3)\,\psi_{2,3,5}(x_2,x_3,x_5)\,\psi_{2,4,5}(x_2,x_4,x_5) {}\times \psi_{3,5,6}(x_3,x_5,x_6)\,\psi_{4,5,6,7}(x_4,x_5,x_6,x_7).
What independencies does the graph imply? Reading the global Markov property off the picture: removing \{3,4,5\} disconnects \{1,2\} from \{6,7\} entirely (every path from 1 or 2 to 6 or 7 passes through 3, 4, or 5), so (X_1,X_2) \perp (X_6,X_7) \mid (X_3,X_4,X_5). Similarly, every path from 1 to 5 passes through 2 or 3, so X_1 \perp X_5 \mid (X_2,X_3).






Note



Practice question. In Figure 3, is X_1 \perp X_4 \mid X_2? Check by finding every path from node 1 to node 4 and seeing whether \{2\} blocks all of them.
Solution. Node 1’s only edges go to nodes 2 and 3, so every path out of node 1 starts by visiting 2 or 3. A path starting 1\to 2 \to 4 is blocked once we condition on \{2\}, since 2 is on that path and is now fixed. But a path starting 1\to 3 \to 5 \to 4 never touches node 2 at all, so conditioning on \{2\} does nothing to it: it stays open. Since at least one path from 1 to 4 survives, \{2\} does not separate them, so X_1 \not\perp X_4 \mid X_2. Separating 1 from 4 would require conditioning on a set that intersects every route out of node 1’s second neighbor, node 3, as well, for example \{2,3\} or \{2,5,6\}.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
section: What MRFs can express that DAGs cannot, and vice versa
text:
What MRFs can express that DAGs cannot, and vice versa
The grid made MRFs look like a strict improvement on DAGs. They are not: the two representations are not nested, and each can express independence patterns the other cannot.
An MRF with no equivalent DAG. Take the 4-cycle A-D-C-B-A shown below (edges A\text{-}D, A\text{-}B, D\text{-}C, B\text{-}C, and no diagonal). Its two non-adjacent pairs give two independence statements simultaneously: A \perp C \mid \{D,B\} and B \perp D \mid \{A,C\}. Any attempt to encode this as a DAG by orienting the four edges necessarily creates a v-structure (a collider) at one of the four nodes, and by the explaining-away logic of Week 2, that collider blocks one of the two independencies while leaving the other intact, or introduces an independence (such as making B and D marginally independent) that was never true in the undirected model. No orientation of the diamond’s edges reproduces both independencies at once.

Figure 4. A diamond MRF. Both A\perp C\mid\{D,B\} and B\perp D\mid\{A,C\} hold simultaneously; no directed version of this graph reproduces both.
A DAG with no equivalent MRF. Conversely, take the explaining-away structure from Week 2, X \to Z \leftarrow Y. There, X and Y are marginally independent (X\perp Y) but become dependent once Z is observed (X \not\perp Y \mid Z). An undirected model cannot express this pattern: the global Markov property says that if X \perp Y holds unconditionally, no set of nodes we condition on can ever create a dependency between them, since observing more variables in an MRF can only add to the separating set, never remove an edge. Collider-created dependence is a genuinely directed phenomenon.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
text:
MRFs as exponential families
So far a potential has been any nonnegative table, and the graph has told us only which variables share a potential. To learn potentials from data we need a parameterized family. Week 1 already gave us one with a complete MLE theory, the exponential family, and this section shows that MRFs fit into it.






Note



Homework-relevant. This section’s log-linear form and sufficient statistics are the same exponential-family machinery from Week 1 (Maximum likelihood estimation in Week 1), applied to potentials instead of a single density. If a current or upcoming assignment asks you to write an MRF or a Gaussian graphical model in exponential-family form, this derivation pattern is the one to reuse.


Consider the parametric family p(\boldsymbol{x}\mid\theta) = \frac{1}{Z(\theta)}\prod_{C\in\mathcal{C}} \psi_C(x_C\mid\theta_C), \qquad \theta = (\theta_C)_{C\in\mathcal{C}}. Taking the log of the product turns it into a sum, exactly as in Week 1’s move from likelihood to log-likelihood: p(\boldsymbol{x}\mid\theta) = \exp\Big\{\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}} \log\psi_C(x_C\mid\theta_C) - \underbrace{\log Z(\theta)}_{=A(\theta)}\Big\}. If each potential has a log-linear form, \log\psi_C(x_C\mid\theta_C) = \theta_C^\top \phi_C(x_C), this becomes exactly Week 1’s exponential family, with natural parameter \theta, sufficient statistic \phi = (\phi_C)_{C\in\mathcal{C}}, and log-partition function A(\theta) = \log Z(\theta): p(\boldsymbol{x}\mid\theta) = \exp\Big\{\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}} \theta_C^\top \phi_C(x_C) - A(\theta)\Big\}.






TipQuestion: Where does the log-linear form come from, and why do we want an exponential family at all?





The core idea. We choose the potentials so that the log of each one is a weighted sum of features of its clique’s variables: \log\psi_C(x_C\mid\theta_C) = \theta_C^\top\phi_C(x_C) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \psi_C(x_C\mid\theta_C) = \exp\{\theta_C^\top\phi_C(x_C)\}. So \psi_C is not \theta times a function of x. Its log is, and \psi_C is the exponential of that (which also keeps it positive). This is a modelling choice, not something derived from the MRF definition. We make it because it is exactly what Week 1’s template needs.
What each object is. For a clique C with |C| variables and d_C chosen features:








Object
Input
Output




x_C
(none)
the values of the clique’s \lvert C\rvert variables, e.g. (x_1,x_2)\in\{0,1\}^2


\phi_C (feature map)
x_C
a vector in \mathbb{R}^{d_C}


\theta_C (weights)
(none)
a vector in \mathbb{R}^{d_C}, one weight per feature


\psi_C (potential)
x_C
a positive number


\log\psi_C
x_C
a real number



Why the transpose. Both \theta_C and \phi_C(x_C) are column vectors of length d_C. \log\psi_C must be a single number, and \theta_C^\top\phi_C(x_C), a (1\times d_C) row times a (d_C\times 1) column, is the dot product \sum_{k=1}^{d_C}\theta_{C,k}\,\phi_{C,k}(x_C): each feature times its own weight, summed. Without the transpose, \theta_C\phi_C would be a column times a column, which is undefined.
Why this makes an exponential family. Run Week 1’s recipe (Exponential families):

\log Z(\theta) sums over all \boldsymbol x, so it depends only on \theta. It plays the role of A(\theta).
Each \log\psi_C mixes data and parameters, so it must factor as (parameters)^\top(function of data). The log-linear form is precisely that requirement, clique by clique. A potential like \psi_C = 1+\theta_C x_C fails, since \log(1+\theta_C x_C) does not split.
A sum of dot products is one dot product of stacked vectors. With \theta\in\mathbb{R}^d and \phi(\boldsymbol x)\in\mathbb{R}^d the concatenations over cliques, d=\sum_C d_C: \sum_C\theta_C^\top\phi_C(x_C) = \theta^\top\phi(\boldsymbol x).

This gives natural parameter \theta, sufficient statistic \phi, h=1, and A(\theta)=\log Z(\theta), a map from \mathbb{R}^d to \mathbb{R}.
Examples. The Ising model (The Ising model) has d_{st}=1: \phi_{st}=x_sx_t and \theta_{st}=J_{st}. For a discrete table, indicator features always work. A binary edge with invented values \psi(0,0)=2, \psi(0,1)=1, \psi(1,0)=1, \psi(1,1)=4 has d_C=4, \theta_C=(\log 2,0,0,\log 4), and \phi_C(1,1)=(0,0,0,1), so \theta_C^\top\phi_C(1,1)=\log 4.
Why we want this. From Week 1:

the data enter only through \sum_n\phi(\boldsymbol x^{(n)}) (clique counts, for indicator features);
\nabla A(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_\theta[\phi(\boldsymbol X)] (Mean of sufficient statistics), so the MLE matches the model’s clique marginals to the data’s clique frequencies;
the second derivative of A is a covariance, so A is convex and the log-likelihood is concave, with no spurious local maxima.

The catch is that Z and its gradient sum over every joint configuration, which is why inference keeps returning in later weeks.



When does the log-linear form hold? For finite discrete x_C, \log\psi_C takes only finitely many values, one per setting of x_C. Let \theta_C list all those values, and let \phi_C(x_C) be the indicator vector with a 1 in the entry matching x_C’s current setting and 0 elsewhere: then \theta_C^\top \phi_C(x_C) just selects out the one matching entry, which is \log\psi_C(x_C\mid\theta_C) by construction. As in Week 1’s exponential-family facts, the log-partition function’s gradient recovers an expectation: \partial \log Z(\theta) / \partial \theta_C = \mathbb{E}[\phi_C(X_C)].
Worked example: minimal vs. non-minimal. Take the chain X_1 - X_2 - X_3 with binary variables, so p(x_1,x_2,x_3\mid\theta) = \frac{1}{Z(\theta)}\psi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2\mid\theta_{1,2})\,\psi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3\mid\theta_{2,3}). Following the finite-discrete construction, index \theta_{1,2} by the four settings of (x_1,x_2): \theta_{1,2} := \begin{bmatrix}\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0)\\ \log\psi_{1,2}(0,1)\\ \log\psi_{1,2}(1,0)\\ \log\psi_{1,2}(1,1)\end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^4, with \phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) the corresponding indicator vector, e.g. \phi_{1,2}(0,1) = (0,1,0,0)^\top. This reproduces \log\psi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2\mid\theta_{1,2}) = \theta_{1,2}^\top \phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) exactly. If the potentials are taken to be normalized already (as the tutorial does), Z(\theta)=1; in general Z(\theta)=\sum_{\boldsymbol x}\exp\{\theta^\top\phi(\boldsymbol x)\}.
But this representation is not minimal: every setting of \phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) has entries summing to exactly 1 (only one indicator is ever “on”), so all four possible values of \phi_{1,2} lie on the hyperplane \{v : v^\top(1,1,1,1)^\top = 1\} rather than spanning \mathbb{R}^4. The tutorial says a non-minimal family fails the gradient identity \nabla A(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_\theta[\phi(X)]. More precisely, the identity still holds for the true log-partition function A(\theta)=\log Z(\theta); what fails is identifiability (different \theta give the same distribution, and A is not strictly convex). The identity only appears to fail if \theta is restricted to the set where Z(\theta)=1, because then A=0 there and the coordinates of \theta cannot vary independently. The fix is to drop the redundant first coordinate and re-express the other three relative to it: \bar\theta_{1,2} = \big(\theta^{(1)},\,\theta^{(2)},\,\theta^{(3)}\big), \quad \text{where} \theta^{(1)} = \log\psi_{1,2}(0,1)-\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0), \theta^{(2)} = \log\psi_{1,2}(1,0)-\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0), \theta^{(3)} = \log\psi_{1,2}(1,1)-\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0), \bar\phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) = \begin{bmatrix}(1-x_1)x_2\\ x_1(1-x_2)\\ x_1 x_2\end{bmatrix}, and analogously for \bar\theta_{2,3}, \bar\phi_{2,3}. This three-dimensional-per-edge parameterization is minimal, and its log-partition function, A(\bar\theta) = \log Z - \log\big(\psi_{1,2}(0,0)\,\psi_{2,3}(0,0)\big), which is -\log\big(\psi_{1,2}(0,0)\,\psi_{2,3}(0,0)\big) under the Z=1 convention, is no longer identically zero. The general lesson: writing every table entry as its own parameter is always possible but wastes one degree of freedom per clique to the normalization constraint; a minimal representation fixes a reference setting (here, (0,0)) and parameterizes only the contrast with it.
